                    PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION OF NEW 16 TAC §25.194


 1   The Public Utility Commission of Texas (commission) proposes new 16 Texas Administrative

 2   Code (TAC) §25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards. This proposed rule will

 3   implement Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) §37.0561, as enacted by Senate Bill (SB) 6

 4   during the Texas 89th Regular Legislative Session. The new rule will implement new PURA

 5   §37.0561, which requires the commission to establish standards for interconnecting large load

 6   customers in the ERCOT power region in a manner designed to support business development in

 7   this state while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system

 8   reliability. The new rule will require a large load customer, before the large load customer can be

 9   included in an ERCOT interconnection study, to execute an intermediate agreement that requires

10   the large load customer to provide certain disclosures and post financial security in the amount of

11   $50,000 per megawatt (MW). The new rule will also require a large load customer, not later than

12   3060 days after ERCOT completes the interconnection study, to execute an interconnection

13   agreement that requires the large load customer to update its disclosures, pay a non-refundable

14   interconnection fee maintain financial security in the amount of $50,000 per MW; post financial

15   security creditable toward the customer’s obligations for significant equipment or services and
      Project No. 58481        (Staff Recommendation) Proposal for Publication                 Page 2 of 48


 1   contribution in aid of construction; pay contribution in aid of construction for direct

 2   interconnection costs; and post financial security for system upgrades., which is independent of

 3   and not creditable against the interconnection security. Additionally, the new rule will set forth

 4   the consequences of withdrawing all or a portion of requested peak demand or contracted peak

 5   demand and the consequences of failing to satisfy a milestone in the large load customer’s schedule

 6   for phased energization. Finally, the new rule will set forth the terms for refundrelease of financial

 7   security for a large load customer that energizes. The new rule will also establish transitional

 8   provisions through applicability designations, integrated within the intermediate agreement and

 9   interconnection agreement requirements, for a large load customer that has executed an

10   interconnection agreement or an intermediate agreement before the effective date of this section.

11

12   Growth Impact Statement

13   The agency provides the following governmental growth impact statement for the proposed rule,

14   as required by Texas Government Code §2001.0221. The agency has determined that for each

15   year of the first five years that the proposed rule is in effect, the following statements will apply:

16   (1) the proposed rule will not create a government program and will not eliminate a government

17   program;

18   (2) implementation of the proposed rule will not require the creation of new employee positions

19   and will not require the elimination of existing employee positions;

20   (3) implementation of the proposed rule will not require an increase and will not require a decrease

21   in future legislative appropriations to the agency;

 6   and

 9   Fiscal Impact on Small and Micro-Businesses and Rural Communities

10   There is no adverse economic effect anticipated for small businesses, micro-businesses, or rural

11   communities as a result of implementing the proposed rule. Accordingly, no economic impact

12   statement or regulatory flexibility analysis is required under Texas Government Code

13   §2006.002(c).

14

15   Takings Impact Analysis

16   The commission has determined that the proposed rule will not be a taking of private property as

17   defined in chapter 2007 of the Texas Government Code.

18

19   Fiscal Impact on State and Local Government

20   Jessie Horn, Sr. Counsel, Rules and Projects Division, has determined that for the first five-year

21   period the proposed rule is in effect, there will be no fiscal implications for the state or for units of
      Project No. 58481        (Staff Recommendation) Proposal for Publication               Page 4 of 48


 1   local government under Texas Government Code §2001.024(a)(4) as a result of enforcing or

 2   administering the sections.

 3

 4   Public Benefits

 5   Ms. Horn has determined that for each year of the first five years the proposed section is in effect

 6   the public benefit anticipated as a result of enforcing the section will be increased transparency

 7   and support of business development. There will be a probable economic cost to persons required

 8   to comply with the rule under Texas Government Code §2001.024(a)(5) because PURA §37.0561,

 9   which the rule implements, requires large load customers to make financial commitments.

10

11   Local Employment Impact Statement

12   For each year of the first five years the proposed section is in effect, there should be no effect on

13   a local economy; therefore, no local employment impact statement is required under Texas

14   Government Code §2001.022.

15

16   Costs to Regulated Persons

17   Texas Government Code §2001.0045(b) does not apply to this rulemaking because the commission

18   is expressly excluded under subsection §2001.0045(c)(7).

22   Texas Government Code §2001.029. The request for a public hearing must be received by April

 4   Public Comments

 5   Interested persons may file comments electronically through the interchange on the commission’s

 6   website or by submitting a paper copy to Central Records, Public Utility Commission of Texas,

 7   1701 North Congress Avenue, P.O. Box 13326, Austin, Texas 78711-3326. Initial comments must

 8   be filed by April 17, 2026. Comments should be organized in a manner consistent with the

 9   organization of the proposed rules. The commission invites specific comments regarding the costs

10   associated with, and benefits that will be gained by, implementation of the proposed rule. The

11   commission will consider the costs and benefits in deciding whether to modify the proposed rules

12   on adoption. All comments should refer to Project Number 58481.

14   Each set of comments should include a standalone executive summary as the last page of the

15   filing. This executive summary must be clearly labeled with the submitting entity’s name

16   and should include a bulleted list covering each substantive recommendation made in the

 1   §25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.

 2   (a)    Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric utility,

 3          a municipally owned utility, and electric cooperative to interconnect a large load customer

 4          to the ERCOT system. Nothing in this section limits the authority of a municipally owned

 5          utility or an electric cooperative to impose electric service requirements for large load

 6          customers on their systems in addition to the standards adopted under this section.

 7

 8   (b)    Applicability. This section applies to a large load customer that seeks:

 9          (1)    a new interconnection that is equal to or exceeds 75 megawatts (MW);

10          (2)    an expanded interconnection that equals or exceeds 75 MW for the first time; and

11                 or

12          (3)    an expanded interconnection that exceeds 75 MW by 75 MW or more.

13          This section applies prospectively and does not require re-study of interconnection

14          facilities or requirements already addressed under an interconnection agreement executed

15          prior to the effective date, except for incremental impacts not previously evaluated.

16

18          meanings unless the context indicates otherwise:

19          (1)    Backup generating facilities -- Generation facilities or energy storage facilities

20                 that are not capable of operating, or are not configured to operate, in parallel with

21                 the ERCOT system and cannot export energy to the ERCOT system.

22          (2)    Competitively sensitive information -- Competitively sensitive information

23                 includes exact site locations, such as parcel identifiers or property boundaries;

 2                 proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-deployment strategies; and

 3                 financing structures. Competitively sensitive information does not include the

 5                 or contracted peak demand; timing of energization; or whether an interconnection

 6                 request is associated with the same applicant or affiliated entities.

 8                 load customer requests that an interconnecting DSP or an interconnecting TSP

 9                 serve at a site as stated in the interconnection agreement.

11                 municipally owned utility, or electric cooperative that is certificated to provide

                    INTERSECT POWER LLC’S INITIAL COMMENTS

                                    I.      INTRODUCTION

       Intersect Power, LLC (“Intersect”) appreciates the Commission’s and Staff’s efforts to
implement PURA § 37.0561 through proposed 16 TAC § 25.194 in a manner that balances
reliability, cost-causation, and continued economic development in the ERCOT region. Intersect
supports the core objectives reflected in the Proposal for Publication (“PFP”), including
establishing a transparent and standardized framework under which large load customers
contribute to the costs of their interconnection while minimizing the risk of stranded infrastructure.

       Senate Bill 6 directs the Commission to establish standards that support business
development while minimizing stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.
Achieving these objectives requires a framework that: (i) aligns financial obligations with actual
cost incurrence and system risk; (ii) preserves regulatory certainty for projects that have already
advanced under existing processes; and (iii) avoids procedural or commercial requirements that
could delay interconnection studies and energization, while preventing distortions to efficient
project development. Accordingly, Intersect respectfully submits that targeted refinements are
necessary to achieve these outcomes. In addition to the comments set forth herein, Intersect is
providing proposed redlines to the PFP based on and building upon the March 31, 2026 redlines
submitted by Schaper Energy Consulting LLC, which reflect the clarifications and refinements
described below.

      II.     PROSPECTIVE APPLICATION AND PROTECTION OF RELIANCE
                                INTERESTS

       The Commission should clarify that § 25.194 applies on a prospective basis only and does
not retroactively apply to projects that have already executed interconnection agreements—
including, for co-located configurations, an executed standard generation interconnection

 agreement (“SGIA”) that governs the relevant interconnection facilities and studies—or otherwise
satisfied applicable requirements and made substantial, non-recoverable financial commitments in
reliance on then-existing rules. The statutory framework under PURA § 37.0561 ties applicability
to new or expanded interconnection requests and does not provide a basis to revisit previously
satisfied milestones. Planning Guide § 9.5.2 confirms that, for co-located configurations, ERCOT
conditions energization on execution of governing interconnection agreements (including an SGIA
where applicable), together with notice to proceed and posted financial security—establishing
these elements as the operative indicators of project maturity and commitment. In addition, under
ERCOT’s interim large load interconnection process (Market Notice W-A032522-01) (the
“Interim Process”), projects advanced based on completion of FAC-002–compliant studies
reviewed by ERCOT and progression toward modeling and energization, reflecting substantively
equivalent study and readiness milestones prior to the implementation of Planning Guide § 9. 1

         As currently drafted, the PFP does not include a clear, global statement of prospective
application. While the March 31, 2026, Schaper comments introduce targeted applicability
provisions, including treatment of pre-existing agreements in § 25.194(d)(12) and § 25.194(f)(11),
those measures are insufficient because they function as narrow carve-outs rather than a rule-wide
prospective standard and do not fully protect projects that have already satisfied prior study,
agreement, and financial commitment milestones from re-evaluation, duplicative requirements, or

due to any deficiency in its prior compliance, but because its executed SGIA and completed studies
do not conform with subsequently adopted interconnection requirements. This risk is particularly
acute for planned co-location configurations where a large load is paired with generation pursuant
to an SGIA that was executed, and under which substantial security was posted, prior to PGRR115

    III.       CREDITABLE AND NON-DUPLICATIVE FINANCIAL COMMITMENTS

        The financial commitment framework should operate as a progressive, creditable, and non-
duplicative structure consistent with cost-causation principles and SB 6’s objectives. As drafted, §
25.194 may require multiple layers of financial obligations—including intermediate agreement
security, a non-refundable interconnection fee, financial security for equipment and services,
CIAC, and system upgrade security—that can overlap with respect to the same facilities or cost
components, creating a risk of duplicative cost recovery or over-securitization. To the extent these
obligations are not clearly delineated and credited against one another, the cumulative effect may
result in disproportionately high upfront financial requirements that could deter otherwise viable
projects, without a corresponding reliability or cost-protection benefit.

        This structure creates a risk of duplicative financial exposure, requiring large load
customers to post multiple forms of security simultaneously for the same facilities or costs. Such
an outcome would increase the cost of capital, reduce project efficiency, and discourage
development, without providing commensurate benefits in terms of stranded cost protection or
reliability.



                                                  4
        Intersect supports the approach taken in the Schaper comments to consolidate these
obligations into a unified, creditable financial security framework. Under that approach, all
amounts posted—whether for intermediate agreement security, equipment and services, or
CIAC—are credited on a dollar-for-dollar basis against a single financial threshold, while system
upgrade security remains a separate, purpose-built obligation tied to actual upgrade costs.

To ensure alignment with SB 6, the Commission should:
      Clarify that all financial commitments are creditable on a dollar-for-dollar basis across
       stages and categories;
      Replace the non-refundable interconnection fee with a creditable financial security
       construct, under which any security posted at the intermediate stage is maintained and
       applied on a dollar-for-dollar basis to actual project costs (including CIAC, equipment, and
       system upgrades), with any additional security limited to incremental, project-specific cost
       exposure;
      Confirm that CIAC and equipment-related payments are not duplicative of other security
       requirements; and
      Maintain independent security only for system upgrades, where stranded cost risk is
       project-specific and demonstrable.

This approach ensures financial obligations scale with actual system impact rather than
administrative sequencing.

       IV.     RECOGNITION OF INTEGRATED PROJECT CONFIGURATIONS

The rule should accommodate integrated project configurations, including co-located generation,
behind-the-meter (“BTM”) arrangements, and private use networks (“PUNs”), in a manner
consistent with cost-causation principles. In such configurations, substantial infrastructure
investment may already have been made under standard generation interconnection agreements or
related arrangements governing facilities and studies at the same point of interconnection (POI).
Planning Guide § 9.5.2 recognizes that, in co-located configurations, the governing
interconnection framework may be established through an SGIA or other such agreements, while
the Interim Process (eff. Mar. 25, 2022 – Dec. 15, 2025) similarly relied on completed
interconnection studies and ERCOT review as the basis for advancing co-located load

                                                 5
 configurations toward energization.

          Absent clarification, §§ 25.194(f)(8)–(10) create a risk that large load customers could be
required to post additional financial security for facilities or capacity that have already been funded
under a standard generation interconnection agreement or equivalent construct. This risk is
particularly acute where generation and load are co-located at a single POI or within a private use
network and share common interconnection facilities. Requiring additional security in these
circumstances would result in duplicative cost recovery, misalign financial responsibility with
actual cost incurrence, and discourage efficient, integrated project design.

To address this issue, the Commission should:
         Clarify that, where a large load is co-located with generation at the same point of
          interconnection and the applicable interconnection facilities and upgrades have been
          funded or secured under an executed standard generation interconnection agreement, such
          prior investments in shared or integrated infrastructure are credited toward any financial
          obligations under § 25.194 to the extent they correspond to the same facilities or capacity;
          and that comparable investments and study-backed facilities developed under prior
          ERCOT interconnection processes, including the Interim Process, are afforded the same
          recognition where they reflect substantially equivalent scope and system impact
         Limit financial security and payment obligations to incremental facilities and upgrades,
          required as a result of the large load’s incremental impact on the system, including changes
          to capacity or operational characteristics, and not to modifications that do not give rise to
          new or increased system upgrade costs or stranded cost risk, and that were not previously
          studied, assigned, or funded under the standard generation interconnection agreement or
          other governing agreement; and
         Preserve flexibility in payment structures, including as-incurred billing with true-up
          mechanisms, to ensure that financial requirements track actual cost development and avoid
          over-collection.

 V.        WITHDRAWAL, MILESTONES, AND PROPORTIONAL RISK ALLOCATION

          The provisions addressing non-utilized capacity, milestone compliance, and the refund of
financial security should be more precisely calibrated to actual cost exposure and system risk,

                                                    6
 while preserving sufficient flexibility to accommodate the development realities of large-scale load
projects.

       With respect to non-utilized capacity, Intersect’s proposed notification framework—
triggered at 18 months for failure to energize at least 50% of contracted peak demand and at 36
months for failure to reach full energization—provides a reasonable mechanism for identifying
potential stranded capacity. However, these triggers should be implemented in a manner that
recognizes phased development schedules and avoids prematurely characterizing capacity as non-
utilized where the project is progressing in good faith. In particular, the rule should expressly
preserve the ability of the interconnecting DSP or TSP to accommodate schedule adjustments
where the Interconnecting Large Load Entity (“ILLE”) demonstrates continued advancement
toward its milestones or provides a revised schedule supported by force majeure or other
objectively verifiable constraints.

       More broadly, the treatment of withdrawal, milestone failure, and financial security release
under §§ 25.194(g), (h), and (i) should be aligned with these milestone constructs and grounded in
proportional risk allocation. As drafted, the rule may result in forfeiture of financial security
beyond the level necessary to cover incurred or committed costs, including through mechanisms
that direct remaining balances to rate base without a clear nexus to stranded infrastructure. This
approach creates a risk of over-allocation of financial burden to large load customers and
effectively converts security instruments into penalty mechanisms, which is inconsistent with the
statutory directive to minimize stranded infrastructure costs while supporting business
development. The refund structure for projects that energize—providing for partial release upon
initial energization and ratable release as phased milestones are achieved, followed by additional
annual releases upon sustained operations—represents a constructive, event-driven framework.
However, it should be clarified and refined to ensure that financial security is released promptly
once underlying cost exposure has been satisfied, rather than retained on a fixed schedule that may
not correspond to actual system risk.

To better align the rule with these principles, the Commission should:
      Limit forfeiture to demonstrated, non-recoverable costs and committed expenditures;
      Require prompt release of remaining financial security once such costs have been satisfied


                                                 7
        regardless of fixed milestone timing;
      Retain stronger forfeiture provisions only for discrete system upgrade security, where
       stranded cost risk is most acute; and
      Ensure that milestone timelines and associated consequences remain commercially
       reasonable and account for phased energization, supply chain constraints, and other
       practical development considerations.

   This approach preserves ratepayer protections while ensuring that financial security functions
as a targeted risk-mitigation instrument, rather than an overbroad or punitive mechanism that could
deter otherwise viable large load development.

          VI.     INTERMEDIATE AGREEMENT AND STUDY PROGRESSION

       The intermediate agreement requirement should function as a mechanism to establish
project credibility and enable efficient study initiation but should not operate as a gating construct
that delays access to interconnection studies. Planning Guide § 9 establishes a sequencing
framework in which studies inform planning; the introduction of intermediate agreement
requirements should not disrupt that structure.

       As drafted, § 25.194(d) introduces a risk that utilities may interpret intermediate agreement
requirements as discretionary prerequisites that delay study initiation pending satisfaction of
commercial or financial conditions beyond those necessary to demonstrate project viability. This
could impede timely study progression and delay transmission planning, contrary to both SB 6 and
ERCOT’s stated objectives in transitioning to a more efficient, batch-based study framework.
